{"id": "20:130/q43", "question": "When does the night prayer become due?", "turns_on": "Whether the obligation attaches at the start, the end, or at the start with intention and later tightening.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q43/p1", "position": "At the beginning of its time.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports this as one opinion."}, {"id": "20:130/q43/p2", "position": "At the end of its time.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports this as another opinion."}, {"id": "20:130/q43/p3", "position": "At the beginning, with intention standing in for performance until the obligation tightens at the end.", "reasons": "Jishumi attributes this distinction to his teachers."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q44", "question": "When does the night prayer time end?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q44/p1", "position": "It runs until dawn.", "reasons": "Jishumi states this limit before reporting disagreements about when its obligation attaches."}]}
{"id": "20:131/q01", "question": "What does extending one's eyes forbid?", "turns_on": "Whether 'extending' describes a lingering gaze itself or grief over the wealth missed.", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q01/p1", "position": "A prolonged gaze of admiration, desire, or attachment to others' worldly goods; a passing glance is excused.", "reasons": "Kashshaf says extending the gaze means lingering without turning away; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurṭubī find it stronger than mere looking. Rāzī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, and Ālūsī excuse a brief glance. Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls fixed sight a metonym for love. Zamakhsharī and Rāzī invoke Qārūn's spectators (28:79–80). Ibn ʿĀshūr says amazement, rather than admiration, is intended; Islāḥī attributes the Prophet's concern to compassion for elites, not greed. Al-Naḥḥās identifies the object of the warned-against look as the unbelievers' worldly allotments."}, {"id": "20:131/q01/p2", "position": "It forbids regret or grief over others' fortune rather than a literal look.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports grief as a second sense; Jishumī reports a regretful gaze. Abū Muslim explicitly opposes a literal looking interpretation in Rāzī."}, {"id": "20:131/q01/p3", "position": "Looking at worldly things one does not need is itself a fault, comparable to excessive speech.", "reasons": "Qushayrī treats unnecessary looking as defective and directs those valued by God to keep every movement within what pleases Him."}]}
{"id": "20:131/q04", "question": "What are the things God gave them to enjoy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q04/p1", "position": "Worldly goods and pleasures, especially the wealth of affluent people.", "reasons": "Mujāhid names the rich. Rāzī and al-Kabīr list sights, sounds, scents, clothes, and marriage. Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī include children, homes, transport, and food; Ibn ʿĀshūr adds gardens, livestock, and women (28:60). Jishumī explains imtāʿ as perceived pleasure and intensive mattaʿa as giving enjoyment; Rāzī says the intensive form suggests repeated abundance. Bursevī links matāʿ to extended benefit or household goods. Al-Naḥḥās specifies wealth allotted to unbelievers."}, {"id": "20:131/q04/p2", "position": "They are God-given resources, entrusted to their recipients.", "reasons": "Islāḥī rejects treating wealth simply as inheritance or intelligence; Bursevī cites a hadith that people are successors watched by God and agents over entrusted wealth."}]}
{"id": "20:131/q09", "question": "How is زهرة read?", "turns_on": "Whether hāʾ is quiescent or opened; some explain the latter as dialectal or a plural.", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q09/p1", "position": "With a still hāʾ, the general or majority reading.", "reasons": "Zajjāj, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn, N​​ashr, and Ibn ʿĀshūr record it; both vocalizations carry the same root sense per Qirāʾāt ER."}, {"id": "20:131/q09/p2", "position": "With fatḥa on hāʾ, attributed especially to Yaʿqūb and other readers.", "reasons": "Jishumī and Bayḍāwī call it a dialect form; Ibn al-Jawzī names Ibn Masʿūd, Ḥasan, Zuhrī and Yaʿqūb; Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī add Abū Ḥaywah, Ṭalḥah, Ḥumayd, Salām, Sahl and ʿĪsā. Qirāʾāt ER says syllable weight changes, not root sense. Ibn Jinnī contrasts Basran restriction to attested glottal dialects with Kūfan extension to pharyngeals; Ālūsī records that Kūfan rule. Al-Naḥḥās attributes the open hāʾ reading to ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar and ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī."}]}
{"id": "20:131/q10", "question": "How is 'زَهْرَةَ' parsed?", "turns_on": "The accusative's governor and its relation to mā, bihi, or azwājan; particular objections turn on definiteness and intervening syntax.", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q10/p1", "position": "An accusative object or result of mattaʿnā, or an implicit 'made/gave.'", "reasons": "Farrāʾ adduces a Banū Fuqʿas poem, though Ṭabarī finds its prepositional governance weak. Zajjāj says God made life a flower for them; Wāḥidī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī and Qurṭubī transmit this. Kashshāf, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Samīn, Bursevī and Ālūsī include a second object or elided verb. Abū Isḥāq, as reported by al-Naḥḥās, relates the accusative to mattaʿnā: God made worldly life a splendor for them."}, {"id": "20:131/q10/p2", "position": "A circumstantial accusative describing mā, bihi, or the granted goods.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya invokes incomplete definiteness; Ṭabrisī transmits Zajjāj's two possible anchors. Qurṭubī prefers ḥāl with dropped tanwīn and al-ḥayāh appositive to mā (36:40); Samīn supports tanwīn elision at two sukūns with poetry. Makkī prefers the ḥāl in Abū Ḥayyān; Ibn ʿĀshūr and Islāḥī use it."}, {"id": "20:131/q10/p3", "position": "An appositive to bihi or its syntactic place.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Samīn and Ālūsī cite it. Ibn al-Ḥājib finds an accusative substitute from a prepositional phrase weak and substitution from a pronoun disputed."}, {"id": "20:131/q10/p4", "position": "An appositive to azwājan, with omitted 'possessors of' or by identification.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Samīn and Ālūsī report it; Ālūsī rejects directly identifying people as enjoyment."}, {"id": "20:131/q10/p5", "position": "An appositive to the syntactic position of mā.", "reasons": "Samīn reports the proposal; Ālūsī repeats it. Qurṭubī objects that li-naftinahum belongs to mattaʿnā; Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān report the same intervening-clause objection."}, {"id": "20:131/q10/p6", "position": "An accusative of censure or specification.", "reasons": "Kashshāf calls it censure or specification; Farrāʾ permits specification of mā or bihi on Kūfan grammar despite the definiteness objection. Ālūsī answers an objection that the world is naturally attractive."}, {"id": "20:131/q10/p7", "position": "An adjective of azwājan.", "reasons": "Samīn reports Abū al-Baqāʾ's objection to a definite adjective for an indefinite noun, answering by tanwīn elision. Ālūsī rejects Farrāʾ's reported adjective parse for the definiteness mismatch."}, {"id": "20:131/q10/p8", "position": "A cognate accusative, considered weak.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī compares ṣunʿ Allāh and waʿd Allāh (27:88; 30:6) but finds this possible parse weak."}]}
{"id": "20:131/q11", "question": "What does 'لِنَفْتِنَهُمْ فِيهِ' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether fitnah is an open test of gratitude and duty, a particular obstacle to faith, or punishment and misguidance.", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q11/p1", "position": "God tests recipients through favors, exposing gratitude or ingratitude.", "reasons": "Qatāda and al-Suddī gloss testing; Wāḥidī specifies gratitude. Jishumī says it distinguishes truthful and grateful from false and ungrateful; Islāḥī contrasts favor testing gratitude with hardship testing patience (20:40). Ibn Kathīr says few thank God. Ibn ʿĀshūr says every provision carries a fitting trial and God thereby establishes proof (23:55–56)."}, {"id": "20:131/q11/p2", "position": "The trial is the harder religious duty wealth imposes.", "reasons": "Jishumī lists alms and duties for property, livestock, enslaved men and women, and also spending, pilgrimage and jihad; Kalbī and Muqātil in Rāzī note easier access to pleasure and sin. Ṭabrisī mentions obedience to truth and wealth's rights. Abū Isḥāq, as reported by al-Naḥḥās, adds that humility is harder for the rich."}, {"id": "20:131/q11/p3", "position": "The trial is the difficulty wealthy rulers face in following an impoverished Prophet.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports the hardship of leaving status; Ṭabrisī stresses the contrast in wealth."}, {"id": "20:131/q11/p4", "position": "Their abundance is a punishment, misguidance, or a route to deserved punishment.", "reasons": "Ibn Baḥr and Abū Muslim name punishment here and hereafter; Ibn ʿAbbās says favors increase disbelief and transgression, preferred by Wāḥidī as fitting unbelievers. Rāzī cites 9:55; Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ālūsī, and Study Quran include punishment in the afterlife. Ṭabrisī cites the saying that the world has not a gnat wing's weight with God."}, {"id": "20:131/q11/p5", "position": "Worldly gifts turn recipients away from their interests.", "reasons": "Māwardī offers this as a possible explanation; Qushayrī details distraction, arrogance, excess, and disobedience."}]}
{"id": "20:131/q13", "question": "What is 'the provision of your Lord'?", "turns_on": "Whether rizq names a future reward, a present material provision, contentment, revelation or guidance, or spiritual sustenance.", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q13/p1", "position": "Paradise or reward stored in the afterlife.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā, Ṭabarī, Wāḥidī, Muqātil in Ibn al-Jawzī, Baghawī, Jishumī, Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, and many others identify it as Paradise or reward. Ibn ʿAbbās says resurrection. Ibn Kathīr cites the promise of 93:5; Study Quran compares 28:60, 42:36 and 20:71–73. Asad also allows spiritual sustenance in the hereafter. Al-Farrāʾ, as reported by al-Naḥḥās, glosses the Lord's provision as His reward."}, {"id": "20:131/q13/p2", "position": "Lawful or modest sufficient worldly provis

ion joined with obedience.", "reasons": "Māwardī contrasts lawful lasting provision with abundant transgressive wealth; Qushayrī contrasts lawful little with unlawful much and remembrance with forgetfulness. Kashshāf says illicit wealth is not called provision; Rāzī adds contentment and patience. Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Bursevī, and Biqāʿī stress lawful sufficiency."}, {"id": "20:131/q13/p3", "position": "Contentment with one's lot and trust in God.", "reasons": "Sula­mī transmits Abū Bakr ibn Ṭāhir's renunciation, an anonymous combination of trust and contentment, and Abū ʿUthmān's reliance over striving; Ibn al-Jawzī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Ālūsī report contentment. Study Quran preserves trust alone and trust with contentment."}, {"id": "20:131/q13/p4", "position": "Prophethood, Islam, and divine guidance.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Ālūsī include these; Ṣāḥib al-Kashf prefers this worldly sense as fitting the context. Islāḥī says revealed nourishment cultivates piety."}, {"id": "20:131/q13/p5", "position": "The Qur'an granted to the Prophet.", "reasons": "Abū Shāmah and al-Sakhāwī say it surpasses others' worldly gifts; Itqān reports the same."}, {"id": "20:131/q13/p6", "position": "Future lands and spoils for believers.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, and Ālūsī report this worldly promise."}, {"id": "20:131/q13/p7", "position": "A gift or allotted nourishment, including spiritual knowledge and illumination.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives the broad gift sense; Bursevī lists worldly or otherworldly shares and bodily food, then inward nourishment by knowledge, wisdom, primordial effusion, and manifestation. Qāshānī names afterlife realities and lights."}]}
{"id": "20:131/q15", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported for this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the narrated pledge marks actual revelation despite the sūra's Meccan setting and the verse's context.", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q15/p1", "position": "Abū Rāfiʿ says a Jewish seller or lender demanded collateral for flour or food, and the Prophet pledged his armor before the verse consoled him.", "reasons": "Accounts differ in whether it was sale, loan or food for a guest, whether Rajab was specified, and whether 15:87 and 20:132 also descended. Wāḥidī and Kashshāf give no grading. Suyūṭī uses the report to propose a Medinan exception. Abū Rāfiʿ, in Wāḥidī's report, specifies a food loan sought for a guest from a Jewish seller, who demanded armor as collateral before the verse consoled the Prophet."}, {"id": "20:131/q15/p2", "position": "The verse belongs to its Meccan context; the collateral incident did not cause its descent.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya argues the sūra is Meccan whereas the pawn occurred late in Medina and the Prophet died with his armor pledged; Qurṭubī reports him. Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds the verse's conclusion incompatible with the story. Ibn ʿĀshūr suggests Abū Rāfiʿ confused recitation of a familiar verse with fresh descent, or that 'descent' meant recitation."}]}
{"id": "20:131/q16", "question": "What reports describe the verse's consolation and its use?", "turns_on": "The separate reported speakers, actions and circumstances.", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q16/p1", "position": "The Prophet or Ubayy warns that failing to accept God's consolation and watching others' goods prolongs grief.", "reasons": "Sulamī reports an ungraded Prophetic saying; Māwardī reports a caller's announcement, Ṭabrisī reports the Prophet sitting upright and repeating the consolation, and Ibn al-Jawzī quotes Ubayy. Ubayy adds that counting only food, drink or clothes as blessings diminishes knowledge and invites punishment; Baghawī adds trust in God prevents regret. Ṭabāṭabāʾī quotes al-Qummī from Abū ʿAbd Allāh that the Prophet sat upright when the verse descended; the excerpt ends before his speech."}, {"id": "20:131/q16/p2", "position": "ʿUrwa recited the verse after seeing rulers' wealth, went home and called his household to prayer.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Jishumī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Rāzī, Qurṭubī, Ibn Kathīr and Durr preserve variants: seeing rulers, visiting rich people, or hearing reports; some say he recited through wa-abqā and prayed. Kashshāf reports ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr seeing rulers' wealth, reciting the warning, and calling people to prayer."}, {"id": "20:131/q16/p3", "position": "The Prophet drew away from impressive camels in response to the verse.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī relates that he covered himself with his garment as he passed the fat, dung-covered camels of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq."}]}
{"id": "20:131/q18", "question": "What ethical counsel is drawn from others' worldly display?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:131/q18/p1", "position": "Believers should avert admiring attention from ostentatious wealth and practice contentment.", "reasons": "Pious scholars in Kashshāf and others say spectators reward tyrants' displays; al-Ḥasan urges seeing sin's humiliation beneath garments and mounts. Jishumī urges little and detachment; Wāsiṭī consoles the poor. A reported hadith counsels comparison with more devout and less wealthy people; Jesus warns that enthroning the world enslaves. Qushayrī's poem disciplines the eye for admiring other than the beloved. Qushayrī likens looking at unneeded worldly things to excessive speech and urges those valued by God to keep every movement within what pleases Him."}, {"id": "20:131/q18/p2", "position": "Worldly ease is no proof of divine favor; lawful goods may be enjoyed and shared responsibly.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu warns against envy while affirming lawful enjoyment, aid to others, endurance of deprivation, and seeking God's favor. Rāzī reports that God looks at hearts and deeds rather than forms and wealth; Abū Ḥayyān cites the world as cursed except what is sought for God. Ibn Kathīr portrays the Prophet sharing all he received and not storing it. The report of ʿUmar contrasts his sparse home with Caesar and Khosrow, whose goods came early."}, {"id": "20:131/q18/p3", "position": "The world's sweetness can enslave and deceive the attached.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites Khujandī's honey with greater bitter trouble, Mathnawī's carrion, and Ḥāfiẓ's seductive bride; Qushayrī cautions that distraction breeds arrogance and excess."}]}
{"id": "20:132/q05", "question": "What does commanding one's family to pray accomplish?", "turns_on": "Which effect of the prayer command the commentator draws out: moral restraint, aid in hardship, worship, or inward discipline.", "positions": [{"id": "20:132/q05/p1", "position": "It restrains wrongdoing and protects the family from punishment.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Baghawī say prayer restrains indecency and wrongdoing; Biqāʿī cites 29:45. Ibn Kathīr connects saving one's family through prayer to 66:6."}, {"id": "20:132/q05/p2", "position": "It gives help through hardship and turns attention from wealth toward worship.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī says prayer helps with hardship and prevents preoccupation with livelihood or wealthy habits. Bursevī directs the poor to prayer rather than gazing at the wealthy; al-Wāsiṭī says the prior warning consoles the poor. Ibn Kathīr and Qushayrī connect prayer with relief and provision; Islahi says vigilant prayer builds perseverance. Al-Zamakhsharī directs the Prophet and his family to prayer for endurance in hardship and focus on the afterlife; he reports Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī urging his poor family to rise and pray."}, {"id": "20:132/q05/p3", "position": "It fulfills the worship God asks for, for the worshipper's benefit.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Abū Muslim cite 51:56–57; Ṭabarī contrasts bodily work with wealth and promises reward. Jishumī, Rāzī, Asad, and Ibn ʿĀshūr say God gains no benefit from the worship; Asad opposes a portrayal of worship as tribute to a jealous God. Ibn al-Jawzī-zād juxtaposes God's command to worship with His undertaking to provide."}, {"id": "20:132/q05/p4", "position": "In an inward reading, it calls the faculties to divine presence and obedience.", "reasons": "Qāshānī takes the family as spiritual and psychic faculties, and prayer as presence, vigilance, obedience, and response."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q40", "question": "How do this verse's signs establish resurrection?", "turns_on": "Initial creation, repeated transformations, revived earth, and further divine attributes.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q40/p1", "position": "The One who first creates humans and revives barren earth can restore dead bodies.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī, Rāzī, Zamakhsharī and many others argue from initial creation to restoration; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says reason establishes possibility and revelation confirms occurrence; Islāḥī adds divine purpose and accountability. The Burhān author also appeals to God's truthful report and power, argues that the Hour entails judgment and judgment requires the Hour, and cites God's revival of dead earth as evidence that He can raise the dead."}, {"id": "22:5/q40/p2", "position": "The signs also establish God's knowledge, free will, and reality against naturalistic or reductive accounts.", "reasons": "Rāzī stresses knowledge and power, rejects reducing the resurrected person to a heart constituent; Qurṭubī says angels are only means and God alone creates; Ṭabāṭabāʾ reasons from divine truth to a lasting afterlife."}]}
{"id": "22:5/q45", "question": "How is the verse linked to surrounding passages?", "turns_on": "Opening warnings, subsequent conclusions, and parallel creation passages.", "positions": [{"id": "22:5/q45/p1", "position": "It supplies proofs for the following resurrection conclusions and continues the opening warning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls 22:6–7 a concluding tailpiece and 22:8 a return to disputants; Study Quran connects the opening's destruction and resurrection to the life cycle; Rāzī cites 36:79 and 17:51. The Burhān author links the dead earth's revival to the Hour and judgment, arguing that each entails the other."}, {"id": "22:5/q45/p2", "position": "The verse connects w

ith other descriptions of creation, aging, and revived earth.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī cites 23:12–13, 64:2, 40:64, 95:4 and 96:2; Study Quran lists many dead-land parallels; Ibn ʿĀshūr contrasts 40:67's mention of old age."}]}
{"id": "33:43/q04", "question": "What does God's ṣalāt upon believers mean?", "turns_on": "The sources gloss divine ṣalāt by mercy, forgiveness, praise, honor, blessing, public good mention, general care, proximity or inward gifts.", "positions": [{"id": "33:43/q04/p1", "position": "God shows believers mercy, compassion and blessing.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā reports Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Ḥasan's Israelite report says mercy precedes wrath. Ibn Qutayba cites verses pairing prayer and mercy; Wāḥidī cites 2:157, as does Ibn Kathīr. Kashshāf and Nasafī appeal to the closing 'merciful.' Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds blessing and beautiful praise; Ibn ʿĀshūr says praise and directing mercy in both worlds. Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it special mercy yielding lasting felicity. Biqāʿī describes compassionate favor. Jishumī reports divine mercy as the first gift in a fivefold account for one who establishes prayer, and as God's part in a fourfold account of ṣalāt."}, {"id": "33:43/q04/p2", "position": "God forgives believers.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī says forgiveness follows obedience. Al-Kalbī says that when God is pleased with a servant He announces forgiveness to the angels and asks them to seek it too. Ibn Qutayba and the paired glosses include mercy with forgiveness."}, {"id": "33:43/q04/p3", "position": "God praises believers, including before the angels.", "reasons": "Abū al-ʿĀliya's explanation, transmitted by al-Bukhārī via al-Rabīʿ according to Ibn Kathīr, specifies praise before the angels. Ibn Kathīr says praise and mercy do not conflict; Ibn ʿĀshūr pairs good mention with mercy. A gloss reported by Jishumī says God praises the believers while the angels pray for them."}, {"id": "33:43/q04/p4", "position": "God honors or esteems believers.", "reasons": "The first three transmit Sufyān's interpretation; Biqāʿī says divine favor and angelic prayer together display the recipients' honor."}, {"id": "33:43/q04/p5", "position": "God blesses believers.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda cites al-Aʿshā's use of the verb. Ibn Qutayba, al-Akhfash, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī combine blessing with mercy or forgiveness."}, {"id": "33:43/q04/p6", "position": "God spreads a good reputation or beautiful mention of the servant among people.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī mark this as another explanation; Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes beautiful praise among divine ṣalāt. The same gloss reported by Jishumī says God spreads the believers' good reputation."}, {"id": "33:43/q04/p7", "position": "God cares for the believers' good and welfare.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī includes making honor visible; Abū Ḥayyān says God wills their good through mercy, and al-Ālūsī prefers the general sense on evidence of the closing mercy clause."}, {"id": "33:43/q04/p8", "position": "God draws servants near.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī starts from prayer as supplication and gives proximity as God's act."}, {"id": "33:43/q04/p9", "position": "God's prayer marks or creates inward faith, truth, purification and contentment.", "reasons": "Abū Bakr ibn Ṭāhir lists faith's light, success, truth, removal of misleading desires and false aims, and contentment in decree. Al-Baqlī describes pre-eternal election in knowledge and love, forgiveness, and appointment of angels while the servant attends to God. Qāshānī describes disclosures of acts and attributes in answer to glorification, since the Essence overwhelms creatures; he cites Gabriel's inability to advance in BURSEVI's parallel account only indirectly. Al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya says eternal prayer precedes and enables remembrance and love."}]}
{"id": "33:43/q05", "question": "What do the angels' ṣalāt and their role mean?", "turns_on": "Whether angelic prayer is described by its petition, its welfare-seeking aim, or its effect.", "positions": [{"id": "33:43/q05/p1", "position": "They supplicate for believers, especially asking God for forgiveness.", "reasons": "The notes vary between general supplication, prayer for mercy, and specific forgiveness; al-Wāḥidī says God commands the request, and al-Kalbī recounts God's announcement of forgiveness. Qushayrī distinguishes sinners' forgiveness and the obedient's beneficence. Biqāʿī adds protection from sins and afflictions and carrying remembrance between God and prophets. Ibn Kathīr cites 40:7–9; Islahi cites 40:7 and 42:5. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 42:5 and 10:3: their intercession needs God's permission. Al-Nasafī quotes their prayer for blessing. Jishumī reports that angelic forgiveness is a gift to one who establishes prayer and is the angels' part in a fourfold account of ṣalāt; another gloss contrasts their prayer with God's praise of believers."}, {"id": "33:43/q05/p2", "position": "Their prayer is intercession for believers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explains that supplication is intercession, authorized by God according to 42:5 and 10:3."}, {"id": "33:43/q05/p3", "position": "They attend to believers' welfare.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī pairs forgiveness with concern for benefit; Abū Ḥayyān says angelic petitions and divine mercy share the intended good."}, {"id": "33:43/q05/p4", "position": "They are treated as bringing mercy because their prayers are answered.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī infer agency from answered prayer; al-Bayḍāwī calls supplication mercy for that reason. Abū Ḥayyān reports the view."}, {"id": "33:43/q05/p5", "position": "Angels watch over believers as well as praying for them.", "reasons": "Study Quran connects this care to believers' remembrance and prayers in 33:41–42."}]}
{"id": "33:43/q06", "question": "What does the single ṣalāt verb mean when predicated of both God and angels?", "turns_on": "The dispute concerns a single common sense, multiple senses in one word, and possible lexical derivations.", "positions": [{"id": "33:43/q06/p1", "position": "It conveys a common concern, inclination or care for the recipients' good, realized differently by God and angels.", "reasons": "Rāzī says mercy and seeking forgiveness imply one shared concern. Al-Bayḍāwī derives shared welfare and honor figuratively from ṣalw. Al-Ālūsī's school uses a general figurative sense because it disallows two literal senses; he allows metaphor from supplication or metonymy from care, and prefers it because the close mentions mercy. Abū Ḥayyān favors shared intended good over al-Zamakhsharī's agency account. Ibn ʿĀshūr says each agent receives the suited implication of one common sense, making homonymy or a general metaphor unnecessary; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it turning or inclination."}, {"id": "33:43/q06/p2", "position": "The one word bears both senses at once: divine mercy and angelic asking forgiveness.", "reasons": "Rāzī finds the reported Shāfiʿī view plausible, including literal and figurative senses together. Al-Ālūsī reports those permitting two senses; al-Samīn says coordination is available on such a theory."}, {"id": "33:43/q06/p3", "position": "Prayer fundamentally means supplication; God's act is mercy, while angels ask mercy or forgiveness.", "reasons": "Language scholars cited by al-Naḥḥās use al-Aʿshā's line and its preceding plea that God spare his father pain and illness. Al-Jishumī says Islamic usage transferred supplication to specified ritual acts. Al-Ālūsī describes a metaphor from supplication through willing good. Ibn ʿĀshūr combines supplication and good mention."}, {"id": "33:43/q06/p4", "position": "Its base is mercy, and its uses belong to one category.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reports Muḥammad ibn Yazīd's alternative derivation."}, {"id": "33:43/q06/p5", "position": "Its mercy sense extends metaphorically from bending in bowing and prostration to tender inclination toward someone.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī describe bodily bending, then kindly turning, then compassion; al-Bayḍāwī offers mercy and spiritual inclination as an alternative."}, {"id": "33:43/q06/p6", "position": "A split-subject analysis assigns mercy to God and forgiveness to angels without giving one word two literal senses.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this agent-based solution and likens it to the split-subject parse; al-Samīn allows coordination under shared meaning or metaphor."}, {"id": "33:43/q06/p7", "position": "A mercy gloss can preserve the verb's distinctive construction and tender sense despite lexical objections.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī answers objectors who say raḥima is transitive while ṣallā takes ʿalā, that their gloss would license 'he had mercy upon him,' and that 2:157 coordinates blessings and mercy."}, {"id": "33:43/q06/p8", "position": "The verb can mean to call out or proclaim.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports al-Akhfash's gloss of yuṣallī as 'calls out.'"}]}

{"id": "33:43/q17", "question": "What does God's mercy toward the believers entail?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize distinct effects and illustrations of mercy.", "positions": [{"id": "33:43/q17/p1", "position": "He guides, forgives, protects, rewards and raises believers by His special mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says obedient believers are not punished. Al-Ṭabrisī says faith causes the great gift of reward. Ibn al-Jawzī says raḥīm is mercy specifically for believers. Al-Bayḍāwī includes welfare, higher rank and angels' care. Qāshānī says perfections accord with readiness. Ibn Kathīr describes guidance in this world away from callers to unbelief and innovation, and protection at the greatest terror with angels' news of Paradise and rescue from Hell. Al-Biqāʿī adds sincerity and higher ranks in Gardens. Bursevī says mercy precedes creation of angels and believers, does not vary with circumstances, and cites a Persian couplet comparing it with a sea unmuddied by floodwater. Ibn ʿĀshūr says mercy exceeds ṣalāt, including all good through words, deeds and kindness. Jishumī reports a five-gift account promising one who establishes prayer God's mercy and great reward in the afterlife, alongside angelic forgiveness and a greeting of peace."}, {"id": "33:43/q17/p2", "position": "He has mercy more profound than a mother's care for her child.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites Anas's report of a mother rescuing her child and the Prophet's assurance God would not cast His beloved into Fire; he judges its chain to meet the two Ṣaḥīḥs' criteria though none of the six books included it. He also cites ʿUmar's report in al-Bukhārī that God is more merciful than a mother."}, {"id": "33:43/q17/p3", "position": "God approves faith and righteous deeds while allowing freedom to disbelieve and sin.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu ties God's mercy to the life He approves."}]}
{"id": "33:43/q27", "question": "What five gifts does one who establishes prayer receive according to the reported account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:43/q27/p1", "position": "Divine mercy, angelic forgiveness, God's mercy toward the worshipper, a greeting of peace, and great reward in the afterlife.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this fivefold account for one who establishes prayer."}]}
{"id": "33:43/q28", "question": "How does the reported fourfold account distinguish prayer by God, angels, the Prophet, and believers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:43/q28/p1", "position": "God's prayer is mercy; angels seek forgiveness; the Prophet intercedes; believers offer greetings.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this fourfold attribution of ṣalāt."}]}
{"id": "35:37/q02", "question": "What does يَصْطَرِخُونَ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q02/p1", "position": "They cry loudly and intensely for help or rescue in Hell.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Ibn Jurayj gloss it as seeking help. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Bayḍāwī connect the plea to ṣarākh, a loud cry; al-Thaʿlabī says ṣārikh can name either supplicant or helper, while al-Qurṭubī distinguishes ṣārikh from muṣrikh and cites a poem about a frightened caller and hoofbeats. Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Nasafī, al-Bursawī and Ibn ʿĀshūr stress the verb's intensity and the sufferers' helplessness. Al-Bursawī also says it is used for seeking intercession. Their following plea explains the cry, according to al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī. Al-Zarkashī says the fuller form yaṣṭarikhūn intensifies the cries beyond yataṣārakhūn. Al-Suyūṭī likewise contrasts it with ordinary yaṣrukhūn. Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares the lengthened endings of 33:66–67, where people stretch their cries in Hell, with the ordinary form in 33:4. Al-Zamakhsharī derives the usage from strenuous shouting and cites a poetic comparison with a pregnant animal crying after its foal is taken away."}]}
{"id": "35:37/q05", "question": "What do the condemned ask to do if brought out?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q05/p1", "position": "They ask to leave Hell, return to worldly life, and replace their former conduct with faith and righteous obedience.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies abandoning association of partners; Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the promised deed as professing lā ilāha illā Allāh; al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī specify belief for disbelief and obedience for sin. Al-Bursawī says deeds require faith; al-Qurṭubī adds following messengers. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the promise belated repentance, with an implicit condition of release. Al-Rāzī says a captive progresses from hope, to request, to a promise of reform. Study Quran relates the plea to 32:12, 19:38, 67:11, 40:11, 6:27, 7:53 and 26:102. Al-Zamakhsharī compares their vow with the appeal in 32:12 to be returned so they can do righteous deeds."}]}
{"id": "35:37/q09", "question": "What does 'other than what we used to do' add to their plea?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q09/p1", "position": "It heightens their regret and admits that their former deeds were corrupt, even though they once mistook those deeds for good.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn citing al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī explain that the apparent suggestion of other righteous deeds disappears once their mistaken self-assessment is recognized; al-Samīn cites 32:12 and 18:104. Ibn ʿĀshūr says they now know their past deeds were false and harmful. Al-Rāzī says the qualification exposes their former corruption, while al-Biqāʿī allows admission of error or regretful recognition. Al-Zamakhsharī says the qualification does not imply other genuinely good deeds, since the speakers were disbelievers and sinners; he cites 18:104 for their mistaken belief that they had been doing good."}, {"id": "35:37/q09/p2", "position": "The contrast allows that their former deeds contained some righteous acts; 'other than' need not declare every previous act devoid of righteousness.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī answers the objection that ghayr contrasts promised righteousness with wholly unrighteous prior deeds by saying their previous deeds were not entirely devoid of righteous acts."}]}

{"id": "35:37/q16", "question": "How is مَن تَذَكَّرَ read?", "turns_on": "Al-Aʿmash's assimilation and the pronounced linking hamza distinguish the alternate reading.", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q16/p1", "position": "The majority reads mā yatadhakkaru fīhi man tadhakkar.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān name the majority reading."}, {"id": "35:37/q16/p2", "position": "Al-Aʿmash reads an assimilated form, reported as mā yudhakkaru or mā yadhkur with man adhkar or udhkira.", "reasons": "The reports vary in transliteration and vocalization; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī say it comes from idhkar and note the unusual pronunciation of hamzat al-waṣl in connected recitation; al-Samīn also records the assimilation and the Shaykh's observation. Al-Zamakhsharī reports mā yudhakkaru fīhi and derives the assimilated form from adhkara."}]}

{"id": "35:37/q41", "question": "How is God's rebuke introduced in the dialogue?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "35:37/q41/p1", "position": "An implied divine speech formula, 'We will say to them,' introduces the rebuking question.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī supplies the unstated 'We will say to them' before God's question."}]}
{"id": "53:34/q01", "question": "What did he give a little of?", "turns_on": "Whether the small gift is the reported payment or ordinary wealth, verbal approval, initial faith or listening, temporary obedience, or a broader spiritual contribution; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the money reading needs a report.", "positions": [{"id": "53:34/q01/p1", "position": "Part of the money or property promised to someone who offered to bear his punishment; he withheld the balance.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says miserliness kept back the remainder; al-Thaʿlabī and others identify the payee as a guarantor. Reports differ on whether al-Walīd had followed, accepted, or merely approached Islam; Study Quran's report reverses the proposed religious exchange, saying he offered a follower money to return to Quraysh religion."}, {"id": "53:34/q01/p2", "position": "A small amount of wealth or charity, followed by withholding or curtailed spending.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk calls it wealth; Ibn ʿAbbās says most was withheld. The ʿUthmān reports describe charity curtailed after a camel and gear were given to his foster brother, then resumed. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads giving as spending. Bursevī says the property was meant as ransom from punishment. Al-Ālūsī allows either 'only a small amount' or 'only a little.'"}, {"id": "53:34/q01/p3", "position": "A little good by speech: praise of the Qurʾān or verbal assent, then silence or inward refusal.", "reasons": "Muqātil speaks of good offered with the tongue; al-Wāḥidī's ʿAṭāʾ and Muqātil specify praise of the Qurʾān, and al-Māwardī contrasts tongue with heart. Reports about Abū Jahl and al-ʿĀṣ likewise describe partial verbal agreement without faith."}, {"id": "53:34/q01/p4", "position": "A brief act of listening to revelation or approach toward faith, then withdrawal.", "reasons": "Mujāhid describes giving of oneself through listening or enjoyment; Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān describes a little movement toward faith. Ibn ʿĀshūr records an inclination toward Islam stopped like digging at rock."}, {"id": "53:34/q01/p5", "position": "A short period of obedience or good conduct, followed by disobedience or cessation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says he obeyed briefly and then disobeyed; Ibn Kathīr attributes the obedience reading also to Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrima, Qatāda and others. Al-Qushayrī reports brief help with jihad as the good conduct that stops."}, {"id": "53:34/q01/p6", "position": "A little of what was due for the afterlife, then abandonment of revelation for worldly life.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī expressly prefers this broader reading to limiting the words to al-Walīd's payment."}, {"id": "53:34/q01/p7", "position": "A small investment of life's capital in the spiritual path, later spent on worldly pleasure.", "reasons": "Bursevī says the seeker tires, returns to the sensual ego, and thereby shows lack of readiness for union."}]}
